newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French insurer Axa's profits jump pre-merger.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French insurer Axa's profits jump pre-merger.

text.p: Axa, which is merging with rival French group UAP to create the world's second largest insurer, on Wednesday said 1996 profits rocketed 40 percent.

Axa's net attributable profit soared to 3.81 billion francs ($670 million) from 2.73 billion on revenues that rose 28 percent to 167.21 billion. It raised its dividend 15.4 percent to 7.50 francs. Earnings per share rose 20.8 percent to 20.36 francs.

Clearing the decks for the merger, UAP reported a loss of 6.45 billion francs after writing off 7.59 billion francs in one-off charges to purge its books and prevent money-losing activities weighing on the new group's future.

Stripping out the one-off charges -- which included cover for businesses in a collapsed property sector as well as the deconsolidation of French bank BNP in its accounts -- UAP's profit was 1.14 billion francs. UAP had a net attributable loss of 2.1 billion francs in 1995.
"UAP is a good company which probably made investments that were a little risky in the past," Axa chairman Claude Bebear, who is heading the new group, told reporters.
"We have taken the last necessary provisions to erase what was done in the past," he said, adding he was confident about the new group's future. "Things are going well."

Axa and UAP, France's two largest insurers, are integrating their operations to form Axa-UAP after a surprise announcement in November that they would combine to create a French heavyweight in the global insurance business. The group will be known commercially as Axa.
Wednesday was the last time that Axa and Union des Assurances de Paris will produce separate accounts. From this year their figures will be consolidated.
Axa shares were up 0.65 percent at 370.60 francs by midafternoon with analysts saying the figures contained no surprises. The results had been widely flagged beforehand.
UAP shares were up nearly 0.9 percent at 146.80.

Axa, widely regarded as the best quality player in the French insurance sector and the driving force of the new duo, said it was aiming for average growth of 15 percent a year in net profit per share between 1996 and 2000.

It said it was seeking return on equity, a key measure of corporate performance, of 15 percent in the medium term and of 11 percent in 1998. It reported return on equity of 10.2 percent in 1996 and 8.5 percent in 1995.

"Axa is now the second largest insurer in terms of size but behind (the Americans) in terms of profitability," noted one analyst. Return on equity among U.S. insurers is around 16 to 17 percent, he said.
Axa said performance was powered by life insurance results, due to a strong improvement in the United States, France and Britain.

It was also lifted by property and casualty insurance results which increased strongly in France, Belgium and Britain. The exception was Axa Global Risks in Britain, which had losses due to strengthening of reserves involving pre-1992 claims.
First-time full-year consolidation of life insurer National Mutual in Australia, consolidated for one month only in 1995, helped drive profits.

There was a hefty increase in income from U.S. financial services -- DLJ and Alliance Capital Management -- and a strong contribution from the holding company thanks to "very good investment results". Its holding had a profit of 148 million francs against a loss of 248 million the previous year.

But some downward pressure on profits came from losses at the Axa Leben life insurance unit in Germany and at French real estate subsidiaries due to real estate valuation allowances. ($ = 5.683 French Francs)
